title: A Lost Land Under the Sea
summary:
Imagine a land almost as big as North America, hidden under the sea. Jerome E. Dobson, a geographer, calls it Aquaterra, a name he first used in 1999. In a 2014 paper, he said this land of about 22.5 million square kilometers may have been home to the first human groups.

During ice ages, water froze into ice, and sea levels fell. Low land now under water became dry, with grasslands, wetlands, and forests full of life. People lived there for most of 120,000 years, Dobson says.

When the ice melted, the seas rose and covered these places. Jericho was a town when seas were about 50 meters lower than today. But older things, like early pottery, may lie deeper.

New finds back up the idea. In 2021, researchers Michael K. Faught and Morgan F. Smith wrote about seven projects in North America. In the Gulf of Mexico, they found burned wood, seeds, and bones up to 9,000 years old. In Belize, they found the outlines of Maya salt-making buildings and a stone object more than 12,000 years old.
why_it_matters: It shows that the first homes of people might be hidden under the ocean, so exploring the sea can help us learn where humans began.

keywords.explanation: A geographer is a person who studies the land and places on Earth.
Aquaterra is the name given to a huge lost land that is now under the sea.
Grasslands are wide open lands covered mostly with grass.
Wetlands are lands where the ground is often wet or covered with shallow water.
Pottery is bowls, pots, and other objects made from baked clay.

background_read: Aquaterra is a name for a huge area of land that is now hidden under the sea.
During ice ages, much of the world's water froze into ice, so sea levels fell and low land became dry land where people could live.
When the ice melted, the seas rose again and covered that land, hiding the places where early people once lived.
Article_Structure: WHO: Jerome E. Dobson, a geographer, and researchers Michael K. Faught and Morgan F. Smith
WHAT: Dobson says a vast land called Aquaterra, now covered by the sea, may have been home to the first human groups, and new underwater finds support the idea
WHERE: In low land now under the sea, including the Gulf of Mexico and Belize in North America
WHY: During ice ages, water froze into ice and sea levels fell, so the land became dry and people could live there; when the ice melted, the seas rose and covered it again

perspectives.description: He says Aquaterra may have been home to the first human groups and that people lived there for most of 120,000 years.
